newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK defends EMU stance after Unilever warning.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK defends EMU stance after Unilever warning.

text.p: Britain's government came under renewed political fire on Wednesday over its attitude to Europe after another major company warned it would rethink its British investments if the country stayed out of a single European currency.

Niall FitzGerald, chairman of Anglo-Dutch food-to-detergents giant Unilever, told the Guardian newspaper that "if Britain absented itself, that would certainly lead to reconsideration of certain investment decisions".

In a statement issued later on Wednesday, he said a decision on Britain's participation on economic and monetary union (EMU) "must be taken with a realistic understanding of the long-term economic consequences and their impact on business".

"To be isolated from this venture could lead Britain to be further detatched from the European core, with all the economic, investment and competitiveness consequences that being on the periphery could bring," FitzGerald said.

His comments followed a similar warning by Japanese motor company Toyota in January and sparked new skirmishes over Europe among Britain's political parties, which are gearing up for a general election that must be held by May 22.

The issue became the latest battleground in the campaign for the Wirral South by-election in northwest England, on February 27. Unilever, one of the largest companies quoted on London's stock exchange, employs around 1,200 people in the area.

Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke told reporters the government was right to keep its options open on EMU. But Clarke, who has resisted strong anti-EMU elements in the ruling Conservative Party, said he doubted the single currency would begin on time on January 1, 1999.

"There are a lot of businessmen and international organisations who hold the view that the president of Toyota gave, or Niall FitzGerald of Unilever is putting forward. But I also think they agree with the position the government has taken," Clarke said.

"We keep our options open, we are actively engaged," he said. "When the time comes, we are going to make a decision about what is best for jobs, what is best for prosperity and what is going to keep investment coming into this country."
The opposition Labour Party, which is ahead in opinion polls by around 20 points, seized on FitzGerald's comments and said Conservative policy was putting jobs at risk.
"The government are directly to blame for putting the jobs of another 1,200 people in Wirral South on the line," said Labour's Jack Cunningham.
"Mr FitzGerald is complaining about the government's deep divisions over Europe," Cunningham said. "That is a much wider issue than just EMU."
Labour said FitzGerald's comments were a further blow to Conservative claims that their stance on Europe was attracting jobs to the country.

Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda said in January his company would shift European investments to Continental Europe if Britain did not join EMU. Fellow Japanese carmaker Nissan has also said that it would prefer Britain to join a single currency.

Both the Conservatives and Labour have declined to commit themselves to signing up to a single currency. The issue has been a thorn in the side of the Conservatives, who remain divided over whether to rule out joining altogether or maintain their wait-and-see policy.
